exceptions_and_traps.title: Tenir à vs tenir de
exceptions_and_traps.description: tenir à means to be attached to or insist on; tenir de means to take after. They are easily confused.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: using à instead of de or vice versa

sources.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir de means to take after someone.
grammar_rules.explanation: tenir de + person means to resemble or take after that person.
usage: To express resemblance to a family member.
restrictions: Only the preposition de is possible; à changes the meaning of tenir
Requires a person as complement, expressing resemblance to that person
conditions: Tenir is used with the preposition de before a person.
The meaning is resembling or taking after that person, usually a family member.
exceptions: Only the preposition de is possible; à changes the meaning of tenir
Requires a person as complement, expressing resemblance to that person
agreement_rules: Tenir agrees with its subject in person and number (elle tient de sa mère).
The preposition de is invariable and does not agree with the person mentioned.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + de + person
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + de + person?
transformations: tenir de + personne -> to take after someone

sources.source_text: De qui tient-elle? Whom does she take after? Elle tient de sa mère. She takes after her mother.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir à means to be attached to something or to insist on doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: When used with the preposition à, tenir means to be attached to (someone or something) or to insist on (doing something).
restrictions: Only the preposition à is possible here; de gives tenir a different meaning
The complement may be a noun, a pronoun, or an infinitive, but not a que-clause
conditions: Tenir is used with the preposition à.
The meaning is being attached to someone or something, or insisting on doing something.
exceptions: Only the preposition à is possible here; de gives tenir a different meaning
The complement may be a noun, a pronoun, or an infinitive, but not a que-clause
agreement_rules: Tenir agrees with its subject in person and number (elle tient à ses bijoux).
The preposition à is invariable and contracts only with a following article (à + les = aux).
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + à + object/infinitive
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + à + object/infinitive?
transformations: tenir à + nom/infinitif -> to be attached to / to insist on

sources.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning. Elle tient à ses bijoux. She is attached to her jewels. Ils tiennent à leurs habitudes. They are attached to their habits. Marc tient à vous voir. Marc insists on seeing you.

Wherever you want to go, you’ll need the verb aller (to go). It is an -er irregular verb, also used in many idiomatic expressions.
Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.
Aller is also used to form the immediate future. So, to talk about what you are going to do, use aller in the present indicative followed immediately by a verb in the infinitive.
The verb venir (to come) and its derivatives, devenir (to become), prévenir (to warn, to inform), survenir (to occur), are all commonly used verbs.
The verb venir (to come) in the present tense + de, combined with a verb in the infinitive, expresses an action that has just taken place.
Another verb conjugated like venir is tenir (to hold)

sources.section_title: The verb faire (to do, to make)
sources.source_text: Another verb you’ll come across all the time is faire (to do, to make).
The causative form is, in most cases, used to express the idea of having something done by someone or of causing something to happen. It is formed with the verb faire followed by an infinitive.
